correctness.rationale: The proof identifies the kernel exactly. Vanishing on the vertical and diagonal lines is equivalent, by invertibility of the \(p\)-point Fourier transform, to the two families of incidence sums being zero; the extra point contributes one scalar cycle functional. The unsigned bipartite incidence rank is \(n_B-c_B\), so a square \(2p\)-column matrix can be invertible only for a spanning connected unicyclic graph. Its incidence kernel is the alternating cycle vector, and the prime cyclotomic minimal polynomial proves that its phase sum vanishes exactly when the two alternating label multisets agree. A fixed Fourier row transformation has modulus \(p^{-p}\), while reduced incidence cofactors are \(0\) off the cycle and unit-modulus on the cycle, yielding \(|\det T|=p^p|S_C|\). The bundled exact modular replay checks 407 finite cases, including all 84 candidates at \(p=3\).

value.rationale: The source highlights this precise family because it is a low-multi-tiling test case for quantitative spectrality. The theorem replaces an unrestricted search through \(2p\)-element frequency subsets of \(\mathbb F_p^2\) by spanning connected unicyclic graphs in \(K_{p,p}\) with one explicit cyclotomic cycle obstruction, and it computes the determinant exactly from that cycle. This is a natural structural reduction of the open example and gives a concrete starting point for optimizing the Riesz ratio without claiming to solve that remaining problem.
